The boundary of what is affordable for the consumer

MEANING

The Budget Line (or Price Line) shows various combinations of two goods which can be purchased with a given income (M) and market prices (Px, Py) when the consumer spends their entire income.

{/* Title */}

MEASURES OF DISPERSION

How Spread Out is the Data?

{/* ═══ WHAT IS DISPERSION? ═══ */}

What is Dispersion?

In the previous chapter, you learned about Central Tendency — Mean, Median, and Mode — which tells us the "center" of data.

But here's a problem: two completely different datasets can have the exact same average!

Dispersion solves this by measuring how spread out the values are from the average. Are most values close to the mean, or are they scattered far apart?

{/* ═══ WHY AVERAGES ALONE AREN'T ENOUGH ═══ */}

Why Averages Alone Aren't Enough

Imagine two students — both scored an average of 50 marks across 5 subjects. But look at their individual marks:

{/* Student A */}
Student A (Consistent)

Student B (Inconsistent)

Mean = 50   |   Range = 55   (High Spread)
Both students have the same Mean (50), but Student A is much more consistent. Student B's marks jump all over the place. Dispersion measures this difference!
{/* ═══ REAL-WORLD IMPORTANCE ═══ */}

Why Dispersion Matters in Real Life

Think about these examples:

{[ { emoji: '🏏', title: 'Cricket — "Who is the better batsman?"', text: 'Player A averages 40 runs (scores: 38, 39, 40, 41, 42). Player B also averages 40 (scores: 0, 10, 80, 60, 50). Who would you pick for a final? Player A — because he is consistent!' }, { emoji: '🌡️', title: 'Temperature — "Which city has better weather?"', text: 'City A: average temp 25°C with daily variation of ±2°C. City B: average 25°C but swings from 10°C to 40°C. Same mean, but City A is far more livable.' }, { emoji: '📊', title: 'Income Inequality', text: 'If the average income of a country is ₹50,000, but some earn ₹5,000 and others earn ₹5,00,000, the data is highly dispersed — indicating inequality.' } ].map((item, i) => (

{item.emoji} {item.title}

))}
{/* ═══ THE FOUR MEASURES ═══ */}

The Four Measures of Dispersion (NCERT)

NCERT prescribes four methods to measure how spread out data is. They go from simplest to most powerful:

{/* 1. Range */}

1. Range

The simplest measure. Just subtract the smallest value from the largest value. Easy to calculate, but it only looks at two extreme values and ignores everything in between.

Range = L - S
{/* 2. Quartile Deviation */}

2. Quartile Deviation (Q.D.)

Better than Range because it ignores extreme values. It looks at the middle 50% of data. Q1 is the 25th percentile, Q3 is the 75th percentile.

Q.D. = Q3 - Q1 2
{/* 3. Mean Deviation */}

3. Mean Deviation (M.D.)

Find how far each value is from the Mean (or Median), take the absolute value (ignore negative signs), then find the average of all those distances. Think of it as: "On average, how far are values from the center?"

M.D. = Σfi |xi - X̄| N
{/* 4. Standard Deviation */}

4. Standard Deviation (S.D.)

The most important and widely used measure. Instead of absolute values, we square the deviations (so negatives become positive), find the average of those squares (that's called Variance), then take the square root to bring it back to original units.

σ2 = Σfi(xi - X̄)2 N

σ = √Variance

{/* ═══ ABSOLUTE vs RELATIVE ═══ */}

Absolute vs Relative Measures

Absolute measures (Range, Q.D., M.D., S.D.) have the same unit as the data (e.g., rupees, marks). But what if you want to compare two datasets with different units or different scales? That's where Relative measures (Coefficients) come in — they are unit-free percentages.

Type Measures Unit When to Use
Absolute Range, Q.D., M.D., S.D. Same as data Single series analysis
Relative Coeff. of Range, Coeff. of Q.D., Coeff. of M.D., C.V. No unit (%) Comparing two series
{/* C.V. Explanation */}

Coefficient of Variation (C.V.) — The King of Comparison

C.V. = σ X̄ × 100

Lower C.V. = More Consistent. If Series A has C.V. = 20% and Series B has C.V. = 35%, then Series A is more consistent (less spread out relative to its mean).

SPEARMAN'S RANK CORRELATION

When Data Can Only Be Ranked

{/* ═══ INTRODUCTION ═══ */}

Qualitative Data

Sometimes, we cannot measure data in numbers (e.g., Beauty, Honesty, Wisdom). However, we can Rank them (1st, 2nd, 3rd). Spearman's Rank Correlation (denoted by R or ρ) is used here.

{/* ═══ FORMULA ═══ */}

The Formula

The formula depends on whether ranks are unique or repeated. For Class 11, we focus on unique ranks.

R = 1 - 6ΣD2} den={N(N2 - 1)} />

Where:

  • R = Rank Correlation Coefficients
  • D = Difference between Ranks (R1 - R2)
  • N = Number of pairs observations
{/* ═══ STEPS TO CALCULATE ═══ */}

Step-by-Step Calculation

Step 1: Assign Ranks

Rank the values of X (R₁) and Y (R₂). Give Rank 1 to the highest value, Rank 2 to the next, etc.

Step 2: Find Difference (D)

Calculate difference of ranks: D = |R₁ - R₂|

Step 3: Square & Sum

Square the differences (D²) and find their sum (ΣD²). then apply the formula.

{/* ═══ SPECIAL CASE ═══ */}

Important Note

Spearman's Rank Correlation is the only method when data is qualitative. It is generally easier to calculate than Pearson's method but slightly less precise for large numerical datasets.

{/* ═══ THE COMPARISON ═══ */}

CPI vs. WPI: The Difference

While both measure inflation, they look at it from different ends of the supply chain. WPI tracks the price at which manufacturers sell in bulk, while CPI tracks the price you pay at the local grocery store.

{/* CPI Details */}

Consumer Price Index

  • Perspective: The Consumer's side.
  • Composition: Includes food, fuel, clothing, and Services (rent, education, medical).
  • Base Year: In India, the base year is often updated (currently 2012 for many series).
  • Usage: Fixing wages and Dearness Allowance (DA).
{/* WPI Details */}

Wholesale Price Index

  • Perspective: The Producer's side.
  • Composition: Primarily manufactured goods, fuel, and power. No services.
  • Base Year: In India, the current series is 2011-12.
  • Usage: Tracking business cycles and industry-wide costs.
{/* ═══ REAL WAGE & PURCHASING POWER ═══ */}

Purchasing Power: The True Value of Money

Purchasing power refers to the quantity of goods and services that can be bought with a unit of money. It is the Inverse of the price index. When the price index goes up (Inflation), the purchasing power of your ₹100 note goes down.

3. Market Trends: Businesses use WPI to anticipate future retail price hikes and adjust their inventory.

CONSTRUCTION METHODS

The Foundation: Simple (Unweighted) Methods

{/* ═══ INTRODUCTION TO SIMPLE METHODS ═══ */}

When to Use Simple Methods?

Simple index numbers are used when we assume that all items in our "basket" have Equal Importance. While this is rarely true in real life (buying 1kg of diamonds is different from 1kg of salt), these methods provide a quick, preliminary look at price movements without needing complex consumption data.

{/* ═══ METHOD 1: SIMPLE AGGREGATIVE ═══ */}

1. Simple Aggregative Method

This is the most straightforward "bulk" comparison. We simply add up the prices of all commodities in the current period and compare that total to the sum of their prices in the base period. The ratio is then multiplied by 100 to yield a percentage.

P₀₁ = ΣP₁} den={ΣP₀} /> × 100

Components:

  • ΣP₁: Summation of prices of all commodities in the current year.
  • ΣP₀: Summation of prices of all commodities in the base year.
{/* ═══ EXAMPLE CASE ═══ */}

Real-World Demo

Commodity Unit 2015 Price (P₀) 2024 Price (P₁)
WheatQuintal₹1800₹2200
RiceQuintal₹2500₹3200
Sugarkg₹30₹45
TOTAL (Σ) - ₹4330 ₹5445

{/* ═══ METHOD 2: AVERAGE OF RELATIVES ═══ */}

2. Simple Average of Price Relatives

Instead of summing raw prices, we first calculate the **percentage change** (Price Relative) for each individual commodity. Then, we find the arithmetic mean of these percentages. This prevents high-priced items (like electronics) from overshadowing low-priced items (like pins) in the final index.

P₀₁ = Σ [ (P₁ / P₀) × 100 ]} den={N} />

Scientific Advantage: This method is superior to the aggregative method because it is independent of the units of measurement. Whether you measure wheat in kg or tons, the "Price Relative" remains exactly the same.

This method uses Current Year Quantities (q₁) as weights. It reflects the cost of what people are buying *right now* at current vs. base prices.

Irving Fisher proposed this method to overcome the biases of Laspeyres (which overestimates) and Paasche (which underestimates). It is the **Geometric Mean** of both methods, mathematically reconciling the two perspectives.

  • Mathematical Precision: Based on the geometric mean, it is less affected by extreme values than arithmetic averages.
  • Consistency Tests: It is the only major index that passes the Time Reversal Test and the Factor Reversal Test.
{/* ═══ COMPARISON SUMMARY ═══ */}
